meta.title: Who really said "A cynic is a man who knows the price of everything and the value of nothing"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Wilde: Lord Darlington says it in Act III of Lady Windermere's Fan (1892). The popular one-line form folds in Cecil Graham's question.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A cynic is a man who knows the price of everything and the value of nothing'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified in Act III of Wilde's Lady Windermere's Fan (1892) — but the words "a cynic" belong to Cecil Graham's question, not Lord Darlington's answer.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and locatable to the line: it is Lord Darlington’s in Act III of Lady Windermere’s Fan ↗, the comedy first performed at the St James’s Theatre on 20 February 1892 and published in book form in 1893. One caveat on wording: in the script the phrase “a cynic” belongs to Cecil Graham’s question, and Darlington answers only — “A man who knows the price of everything and the value of nothing.”

source.heading: The source, in full
source.excerpt:
LORD DARLINGTON. What cynics you fellows are!

CECIL GRAHAM. What is a cynic? [Sitting on the back of the sofa.]

LORD DARLINGTON. A man who knows the price of everything and the value of nothing.

CECIL GRAHAM. And a sentimentalist, my dear Darlington, is a man who sees an absurd value in everything, and doesn’t know the market price of any single thing.
trail: Primary text, twice. Wikisource’s Act III ↗ and Project Gutenberg’s full play ↗ (transcribed from a Methuen & Co. printing, sixteenth edition, 1917) both carry the exchange verbatim, with Graham’s question and Darlington’s reply.

Specialist check. Wikiquote’s Oscar Wilde page ↗ places the line in its sourced Lady Windermere’s Fan (1892), Act III section — not in Misattributed or Disputed. Quote Investigator has no article on it, which is consistent with a quotation nobody needed to rescue.
Dates. Wikipedia ↗ gives the premiere as 20 February 1892 at the St James’s Theatre and the book publication as 1893, by The Bodley Head in London.

The earlier form. Wilde had already used the epigram in chapter 4 of The Picture of Dorian Gray ↗, where Lord Henry Wotton says “Nowadays people know the price of everything and the value of nothing.” That novel ran in Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine in July 1890 and was revised for book publication in 1891 — both before the play opened.
source.excerptNote: Graham’s answering definition of the sentimentalist is almost always dropped when the line is quoted — which is what turns a two-sided joke into a one-sided verdict.
source.rightsNote: Lady Windermere’s Fan was first published in book form in 1893, far earlier than the 1931 threshold that governs US public-domain status, and Wilde died in 1900 — the play’s text is in the public domain in the United States. It is written in English, so no translation rights are involved; the Project Gutenberg ↗ and Wikisource transcriptions are freely reusable.

author.name: Oscar Wilde
author.heading: Who was Oscar Wilde?
author.bio: Born in Dublin on 16 October 1854 and dead in Paris on 30 November 1900, Wilde was an Irish author, poet and playwright who became one of the most popular and influential dramatists in London in the early 1890s. Lady Windermere’s Fan was the first of the society comedies that made him a commercial force: it opened in February 1892 and toured the country for months, even as conservative critics sniffed at it. He is one of the most misquoted writers in English — which makes the lines that are his, like this one, worth pinning down precisely.

misattribution.heading: The author is right. The wording drifts.
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare Wilde blockbusters that survives verification — so the interesting failures here are not about who but about what and where. Three recurring slips:

items.who: Oscar Wilde, recast as one sentence
items.why: The circulating form is “A cynic is a man who knows the price of everything, and the value of nothing” — that is how Goodreads prints it ↗, credited to Wilde with no work named at all. In the script, “a cynic” is Cecil Graham’s question and Darlington replies only “A man who knows the price of everything and the value of nothing” ↗.

Quote-image sites circulate “A fool knows the price of everything and the value of nothing” ↗ over Wilde’s name. It inverts the point: Wilde was defining the person who is too knowing, not the person who is stupid.

The two are constantly conflated because Wilde wrote both. The novel’s version is a different sentence in a different mouth — Lord Henry Wotton’s “Nowadays people know the price of everything and the value of nothing” ↗, in chapter 4. If you are quoting the cynic definition, the source is the play.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution holds: the words are Lord Darlington’s in Act III of Lady Windermere’s Fan ↗, a play Wilde wrote — so quote it as dialogue he wrote, not as an aphorism he offered in his own voice.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: Wilde liked the joke enough to use it twice. It first reached print in The Picture of Dorian Gray, where Lord Henry Wotton, late because he had been haggling over old brocade in Wardour Street, sighs that “Nowadays people know the price of everything and the value of nothing” ↗ — the novel ran in Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine in July 1890 and was revised for book publication in 1891. By the time Lady Windermere’s Fan opened in February 1892, Wilde had sharpened the grumble into a definition and handed it to a character who is himself half a cynic.

On stage it is not a moral verdict but one move in a duel. Darlington needles the room — “What cynics you fellows are!” — Graham asks him to define the term, and the moment Darlington does, Graham fires back a matching definition of the sentimentalist. That second half is almost never quoted, which is why the line now reads as sincere social criticism rather than as drawing-room fencing.

CECIL GRAHAM. And a sentimentalist, my dear Darlington, is a man who sees an absurd value in everything, and doesn’t know the market price of any single thing.
context.pull: Wilde wrote both halves of the argument; posterity kept only the half that flatters the reader.
